metadata.title: Claude, Graphing.
metadata.purpose: Answer one real question in the Teardown register: does Claude already know how to make a good chart, or does a kit have to hand it judgement defaults? Take the graphing kit apart — five primitives, three data helpers, a four-step workflow — and judge where it succeeds on its own terms and where it silently doesn't. Lands the carry-out that Claude only dodges the edges the kit actually marks.

beats.narration_text: Assumption: Claude already knows how to make a good chart. It doesn't — it reads a kit before drawing that tells it what to check. Here's what the kit spells out, and where it stops helping.

beats.narration_text: Here's what's actually in the kit. Five primitives and three data helpers. theme sets matplotlib rcParams and returns resolved colors — the key move is that foreground colors derive from background luminance, so pass a dark background and you get a correct dark chart automatically, no override. palette builds n colors from a base hex, cycles a list, or falls back to the series defaults. finish adds the typographic frame — left-aligned bold title, muted subtitle, provenance caption. save writes PNG, SVG, or both and returns paths. write_html produces a self-contained interactive page by inlining React, ReactDOM, react-is, and Recharts from a local third-party directory — the file opens offline, no CDN dependency. That last choice is a philosophy: they optimized for a chart that still works when the network doesn't, at the cost of a bigger single file. The three data helpers each target a specific failure mode. zero_fill_days fills calendar gaps in a timeseries — skip it when zeros would be a lie because the data is sparsely sampled, not absent. rolling_mean is trailing; early points average whatever exists so far — do not center it. log_floor gives a lower bound for bar charts on log scales, value equal to the axis minimum. All three are optional; use them only when they fit. And the absolute path to graphing's scripts directory has to go into sys.path — not relative, because the working directory is the user's project, not the kit's.

props.sparkLine: theme() derives colors from luminance. write_html inlines offline. zero_fill_days: skip if zeros would lie.

beats.narration_text: Now the workflow. Four steps: look at the data and decide what it deserves; infer colors from context — tailwind config, CSS variables, brand guidelines, semantic meaning; write the script; render and look at the result before handing it over. The render-and-look step is explicit: check labels for legibility, nothing overlapping, colors distinguishable, the story of the data visible. Fix and re-render until it's right. That last step is the honesty test — most tools stop at 'the script ran'; this one insists you look at the pixels. The judgement section gives defaults with explicit permission to deviate when the data argues for it, which is the right shape — a rule that names its exceptions is a rule you can trust. Five defaults worth knowing. Rotate x labels only when they would otherwise collide — short labels stay horizontal. Cap bar width when there are few categories. Label bars with their values when there are roughly a dozen or fewer. Rank categorical bars by value unless the categories have a natural order. A title states what the chart shows — not the chart type, not the column name. Legends only when there is more than one series. Annotate the chart with what matters — a deploy line, a threshold, the peak, the anomaly. An annotation the reader did not need is clutter.

props.sparkLine: Four steps: look, infer, write, look again. Rank bars. Label small datasets. Annotate what matters.

beats.narration_text: So does the kit fix Claude's chart problems? Not exactly. Where it spells something out plainly — the first-step judgment call, colors that adapt to the background, an offline file that just works — Claude follows it and skips the mistake entirely. Where the guidance is a placeholder string swapped by hand, or one phrase covering an edge case, Claude can still get it wrong, the same way a person skimming the same page would. The pattern is worth naming: clarity is contagious, and so is ambiguity. What the kit marks, Claude notices; what it buries, Claude misses.

props.sparkLine: Clear defaults get followed. Buried ones don't.
leftItems: "look at the data, decide what it deserves" forces chart-type judgment from shape
theme() derives colors from background luminance — dark bg, correct dark chart, no override
write_html inlines React + Recharts locally — opens offline, no CDN
each data helper states exactly when to skip it
rightItems: sys.path needs an absolute path — the example itself shows /path/to/graphing/scripts
GRID and ACCENT in the interactive template are literal strings, not variables

beats.narration_text: The honest verdict: a charting kit doesn't give Claude good taste. It hands Claude judgement defaults to start from and a few sharp edges marked — and Claude only dodges the edges the kit actually marks.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here's a prompt you can paste directly into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini. Give it a small dataset you want to chart. Before it writes any chart code, ask what shape the data is — categorical, timeseries, distribution, comparison — what chart type that shape deserves, where the colors should come from, and whether there are any gaps where a zero would be a lie. Then have it render the PNG, look at the image itself, and say what it would fix before handing it back. Go deeper: swap the same data into a chart type its shape doesn't deserve — a bar for a timeseries, a pie for a comparison — and ask Claude what specifically breaks and why.

llm_exercise.prompt: I have a small dataset I want to chart — [paste the CSV, or describe the columns and a few rows]. Before you write any chart code, tell me: (1) what shape is the data — categorical, timeseries, distribution, or comparison; (2) what chart type does that shape deserve, and why; (3) where should the colors come from — a brand palette, semantic meaning, or a sensible default; (4) are there gaps where a zero would be a lie (sparsely sampled, not actually absent). Then write the script, render a PNG, and open the image. Look at it and tell me what you'd fix — label collisions, missing annotations, a legend that shouldn't be there, a title that names the chart type instead of what it shows — before handing it to me.
llm_exercise.dig_deeper: Go deeper: swap the same data into a chart type its shape doesn't deserve — a bar for a timeseries, a pie for a four-way comparison — and ask Claude what specifically breaks and why. That's the fastest way to see what the kit's judgement defaults are actually protecting you from.
